corrected_value.title: The acquisition of abstract words by young infants.

decisions.quote: While the study was not designed to test the difference between noun and verb acquisition, 6–9-month-olds did perform well on one of the two verb pairs ( hug - eat ), contrary to their poor performance on a broader set of non-nouns in a prior study ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2013 ). Whether infants’ apparent success on hug-eat represents random item variation, or a first fragile glimmer of infants’ understanding of these verbs, is unclear, particularly given infants’ failure to demonstrate understanding of kiss-drink here.
decisions.reason: The replicating study empirically re-tests findings from Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) (DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2013.02.011) in a new sample of 6–16-month-old infants using paired dynamic video stimuli: it explicitly repeats the hug-eat verb pair tested in Bergelson & Swingley (2013b), tests whether 6–9-month-olds' prior failure on non-nouns in that dynamic-video study was due to dynamic video presentation versus word class, and re-tests the non-linear comprehension boost around 13–14 months reported in both Bergelson & Swingley (2012) and (2013b). Both the Works Cited list and Crossref metadata verify the identity of Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) in Cognition 127(3), 391–397. The sole shipped original (input_row_index 391, Bergelson & Swingley, 2012, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1113380109) is a separate PNAS article testing concrete food and body-part nouns with static images, and sibling missing target_index 4 (Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012, DOI 10.1111/j.1532-7078.2011.00084.x) is a distinct Infancy study on body-part nouns; report equivalence does not apply. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work.

decisions.quote: In an extension to EEG, Parise and Csibra (2012) demonstrated that 9-month-olds show an N400 mismatch effect when a revealed object (shown as a still image) does not match the word just uttered by infants’ mothers. The items were common objects familiar to children, e.g. banana , bunny , socks . This work contributes an important confirmation that using a different method, infants demonstrate word comprehension at 9 months. However, younger infants were not tested, and surprisingly, even at 9 months infants showed no recognition response when hearing a voice other than their mother's.
decisions.reason: The primary source positively establishes Parise and Csibra (2012) (DOI 10.1177/0956797612438734) as background convergent literature—an earlier EEG N400 mismatch extension using still images of objects (e.g., banana, bunny, socks) with 9-month-olds—rather than an empirically re-tested target. Although Parise & Csibra (2012) appears in the five-study parenthetical summarizing prior reports that infants under 10 months understand words, the present paired-video eye-tracking experiment does not test EEG N400 responses, maternal-versus-unfamiliar voice effects, or Parise & Csibra's stimulus set; instead, the study design and Methods specify that it re-tests early common-noun comprehension and the 13–14-month boost from shipped input_row_index 391 (Bergelson & Swingley, 2012), the overlapping verb stimuli and non-noun video contrast from missing target_index 1 (Bergelson & Swingley, 2013b), and the hand-feet paired-video noun comparison from missing target_index 4 (Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012). Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent.

decisions.quote: The present work is methodologically closest to two studies by Tincoff and Jusczyk (1999 , 2012) . These authors demonstrated that 6-month-olds understand two pairs of words: “hand” and “feet” (2012) and the proper names “Mommy” and “Daddy” (1999). In these experiments, infants were shown a single pair of videos depicting these items. The “Mommy” and “Daddy” were presented live on screen, and the “hand” and “feet” moved a bit in the image. While one video was named, infants’ eyegaze was measured; infants looked more at the matching video.
decisions.reason: Tincoff and Jusczyk (1999) (DOI 10.1111/1467-9280.00127) tested 6-month-olds' comprehension of the proper names 'Mommy' and 'Daddy' using videos of parents, whereas the present experiment tests common concrete nouns (objects and body parts, explicitly excluding whole people from the noun videos) and two verb pairs, with no proper-name stimuli. As the Introduction and Materials explicitly state, the only re-tested noun pair from Tincoff and Jusczyk's paired-video work is hand-feet from Tincoff & Jusczyk (2012) (retained as missing target_index 4), alongside the common-noun and developmental findings of shipped input_row_index 391 (Bergelson & Swingley, 2012) and the verb/non-noun findings of missing target_index 1 (Bergelson & Swingley, 2013b). Thus Tincoff & Jusczyk (1999) is cited as a methodological precursor and part of the broad early-comprehension background rather than an empirically re-tested target. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent.

corrected_value.title: Six-Month-Olds Comprehend Words That Refer to Parts of the Body.

decisions.quote: The words we tested had some overlap with previous work, but only one pair of nouns (hand-feet) had been tested before with young infants, as either still images or video clips ( Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012 ). We also included two pairs of verbs, one of which was tested in Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) . Thus, this study set out to replicate the basic finding of previous work, i.e. that young infants understand common nouns, while also extending the range of the words tested, and their format of presentation.
decisions.reason: The study explicitly re-tests Tincoff and Jusczyk's (2012) paired-video finding that young infants (6–9 months) comprehend the body-part noun pair hand-feet by including hand-feet as one of the six yoked video pairs in its eye-tracking task and confirming early comprehension in a new sample of infants. Both the Works Cited list and Crossref metadata verify Tincoff & Jusczyk (2012) in Infancy 17(4), 432–444 (DOI 10.1111/j.1532-7078.2011.00084.x). This work is completely distinct in authors, journal, and stimulus design from the sole shipped original (input_row_index 391, Bergelson & Swingley, 2012, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1113380109) and from sibling missing target_index 1 (Bergelson & Swingley, 2013b, DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2013.02.011); report equivalence does not apply. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent.

corrected_value.title: Machine learning to analyze single-case graphs: A comparison to visual inspection.

decisions.quote: A secondary purpose was to replicate and extend Lanovaz and Hranchuk (2021) by examining correspondence between visual inspection, the conservative dual-criteria method, and the machine-learning algorithms on a novel dataset. We extended both studies by using clinical data and adding a 10-point scale with definitional criteria to visual-inspection ratings.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly define replicating and extending Lanovaz and Hranchuk (2021) as a secondary purpose, apply the support vector classifier developed by Lanovaz and Hranchuk (2021) to 198 clinical AB phase comparisons rated by five expert visual analysts and the conservative dual-criteria (CDC) method, and directly compare rater agreement, classifier correspondence, and Phase A length effects against Lanovaz and Hranchuk's (2021) simulated-data findings in the Results and Discussion. Both the parsed reference list and Crossref metadata verify Lanovaz & Hranchuk (2021) in Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis 54(4), 1541–1552 (DOI 10.1002/jaba.863). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 803, Wolfe et al., 2018, DOI 10.1002/jaba.453) is an independent 2018 study by different authors comparing expert visual inspection with the CDC method on 31 published multiple-baseline graphs without machine learning; report equivalence does not apply. Prior adjudication (b7a3e244f38db85863a27b1acc63a1cfe4c6a6edd6e8265c7d9f8ff315ff5c18.json) was read and is consistent with this independent verification; the prior state file was absent.

corrected_value.authors: Borreggine, K. L., & Kaschak, M. P.
corrected_value.title: The action–sentence compatibility effect: It's all in the timing.

decisions.quote:
As a first step in assessing the replicability of motor
compatibility effects, we conducted a pre-registered, multi-lab
replication of the ACE. We used an adapted version of the
original ACE paradigm (Glenberg & Kaschak, 2002) that was
used in Borreggine and Kaschak (2006). The choice of this
particular version of the ACE paradigm was somewhat arbitrary. We had no strong a priori reasons to expect that one
paradigm or the other would produce a stronger or more reliable ACE. Ultimately, we chose the Borreggine and Kaschak
(2006) paradigm over the original Glenberg and Kaschak
(2002) paradigm in part because we sensed that this paradigm
would be slightly easier to execute across a large group of
labs.
decisions.reason: The multi-lab replication explicitly selects and executes the adapted auditory-sentence and visual-cue Action-sentence Compatibility Effect (ACE) paradigm and critical sentences from Borreggine and Kaschak (2006) over the original written-sentence paradigm of Glenberg and Kaschak (2002), testing the Sentence Direction by Response Direction interaction on lift-off latency across 18 labs (N = 1,278) and concluding in the Discussion that 'this version of the ACE paradigm does not reliably produce the predicted motor compatibility effect.' Under the codebook replication-chain rule, Borreggine and Kaschak (2006) (Cognitive Science, 30, 1097–1112; no DOI printed in the source reference entry) is the closest target directly re-tested by this study. It is a distinct study published four years later in a different journal with different materials and response-cueing procedure than the sole shipped original (input_row_index 519, Glenberg & Kaschak, 2002, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 9, 558–565, DOI 10.3758/bf03196313), so report equivalence does not apply. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent.
